Their agreement to include Otunnu in the Security Council’s 30 July straw poll before he could participate in a husting organised by the General Assembly provoked diplomatic blowback from advocates pushing for a fair and transparent process, including from the president of the General Assembly herself. 48 Letter from the president of the General Assembly to the president of the Security Council for July , 28 July 2026; “ Letter to the president of the General Assembly and president of the Security Council for July 2026”, 1 for 8 Billion, 29 July 2026. A-Baki’s entry four days before the second straw poll heightened anxieties that new candidates could parachute into the race shortly before a vote to avoid prolonged public scrutiny. 49 A-Baki did appear in a public meeting with the General Assembly and an informal dialogue with the Security Council before its 21 August straw poll. How the Council’s permanent members balance their prerogatives over the push for transparency could affect the next Secretary-General’s political credibility before she or he assumes the office. III. Ten Challenges for the UN Even as the UN is mired in interlocking difficulties, the organisation can still contribute to conflict resolution and crisis management in many domains. The following list features countries and issue areas where the UN confronts either major challenges or opportunities in the year ahead. It is intended to demonstrate the myriad factors affecting how the UN and its member states respond to conflicts and emergencies around the world. The list is not exhaustive, however, and it excludes cases that Crisis Group has highlighted elsewhere or in years past, such as Afghanistan, the DRC, South Sudan, Ukraine and others. 1. Continuing UN engagement in southern Lebanon In August 2025, the U.S. and Israel strong-armed the Security Council into shutting down the UN peacekeeping mission in southern Lebanon (UNIFIL) – first established in 1978 and significantly upgraded by Resolution 1701 twenty years ago – by the end of 2026 (though the phased withdrawal of troops will extend considerably past 31 December). 50 “ Resolution 2790 ”, UNSC S/RES/2790, 28 August 2025. While questions about southern Lebanon have long vexed the Council, the latest conflagration between Israel and Hizbollah raises the stakes even higher. 51 Heiko Wimmen and David Wood, “ Entrenching a Meaningful Israel-Lebanon Ceasefire ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 19 June 2026. The danger is now that the UN will terminate its 48-year blue helmet operation without clarity on what kind of international presence, if any, might follow. Much will now depend on the trajectory of U.S.-backed negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, which to date have failed to produce a viable security arrangement. The two states signed a “framework agreement” on 26 June, under which the Lebanese army is to assert control of “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon, ensuring that Hizbollah no longer has a military footprint in these areas. 52 “ Trilateral Framework Between the United States of America, the State of Israel and the Republic of Lebanon ”, U.S. Department of State, 26 June 2026. Yet the scheme, which is meant to “serve as the mechanism for phased and verified (Israeli) redeployments”, has already run into trouble. 53 Ibid. Lebanon complains that Israel has kept attacking Lebanese territory, including with lethal airstrikes and the systematic destruction of villages, and authorised “pilot zones” only in areas that it never occupied. Israeli officials, for their part, make Hizbollah’s full disarmament a condition for the Israeli army’s withdrawal. 54 Maayan Lubell and Maya Gebeily, “ After US criticism, Israel ties Lebanon withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament ”, Reuters, 13 August 2026. Beirut officially outlawed Hizbollah’s military activities in March, but, in practice, it cannot risk trying to compel the group to disarm. 55 Lebanese political and military leaders have resisted calls to deploy the Lebanese army to confront Hizbollah by force. They fear that such a move could trigger disastrous domestic consequences, such as the military fracturing along sectarian lines. Crisis Group Middle East Briefing N°94, Containing Domestic Tensions in War-hit Lebanon , 27 February 2025. See also Michael Young, “ Pushing Beirut into an armed conflict with Hezbollah is insane ”, Diwan (blog), Carnegie Middle East Center, 14 May 2026. Even if the terms of the deal were to be spelled out more precisely, the belligerents would almost certainly refuse to sign up to the underlying bargain. Hizbollah rejects the direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations outright, insisting that Lebanon entrust Iran, the group’s patron, with securing a full Israeli withdrawal as part of Tehran’s negotiations with Washington. 56 “ Hezbollah insists on linking Lebanon to Iran-U.S. negotiations ”, Asharq al-Awsat , 13 July 2026. Though Israel has participated in the trilateral talks with Lebanon and the U.S., it refuses to accept another arrangement like Resolution 1701, under which its troops withdrew from Lebanon after the 2006 war while Hizbollah remained under arms. Debates about a future international presence will also be shaped by U.S. and Israeli scepticism. Israel has long questioned the value of UNIFIL in helping Lebanon constrain Hizbollah, and it has shown little appetite for a replacement that might obstruct its own military operations. The U.S. does not oppose an international mission per se, but it is wary of replicating a UNIFIL model that it deems ineffective. 57 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and UN officials, Beirut, July 2026. The U.S. and its Israeli partners have long argued that UNIFIL has failed to deter Hizbollah military operations south of the Litani River (even if it has no mandate to confront the militant group by force) and is too expensive. For background, see David Wood, “ Helping UNIFIL Restore Stability in Southern Lebanon ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 August 2025. Washington has sidelined the monitoring mechanism attached to the November 2024 ceasefire, in which UNIFIL and France (the Council’s penholder on Lebanon) were represented. Instead, an annex of the June framework agreement provides for a U.S.-headed “military coordination group”, through which Israel and Lebanon will manage tasks that UNIFIL or a successor force might have helped tackle, including “deconfliction, verification and overall implementation”. 58 The parties did not officially release this annex to the framework agreement, but they have not challenged the authenticity of a text leaked to the media in late June. “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, L’Orient Today , 29 June 2026. Other Council members and Lebanon strongly favour retaining an international presence, having reluctantly agreed to UNIFIL’s termination at the end of 2026 to avoid a U.S. veto that would have abruptly ended the mission in August 2025. 59 “ UN Interim Force in Lebanon: Vote on Final Mandate Renewal and Drawdown* ”, Security Council Report, 28 August 2025; Jamie Prentis, “ Lebanese MPs urge UN to extend peacekeeping mission ”, The National , 24 July 2026. The framework agreement does not mention the UN or Security Council resolution 1701. The annex, however, proposes a future role for a “mutually agreed-upon third-party entity” to verify that non-state armed groups have been cleared from each “pilot zone”. 60 “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, op. cit. To date, Israeli, Lebanese and U.S. negotiators have struggled to flesh out what such verification would entail, making it difficult for interested nations to commit troops to a mission that might prove dangerous. Yet even if the framework agreement eventually falls by the wayside, any other attempt to reach a deal that would link Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon and cessation of airstrikes with an end to Hizbollah attacks on Israel and disarmament of the group would in all likelihood hinge on some sort of third-party verification. International partners have begun debating options for a new multinational presence. In June, the Secretary-General proposed a follow-up UN mission involving both armed and unarmed troops. 61 The report, mandated by the Security Council in Resolution 2790, proposed three different deployment sizes: the largest option would entail 5,525 uniformed personnel, the middle one 3,370 and the lightest footprint approximately 1,980. See “ Letter dated 1 June 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/453, 1 June 2026. France and Italy have also announced plans to create a new multinational coalition in southern Lebanon as a successor to UNIFIL. 62 “ Lebanon president welcomes French, Italian efforts to form coalition to succeed UNIFIL ”, Arab News , 26 June 2026. In parallel, the European Union is weighing a separate mission comprising civilian and military personnel to advise and possibly train Lebanese forces – outside southern Lebanon – in addition to the €180 million it has already committed to support the Lebanese army. 63 Louay Faour, “ European powers seek greater role in south Lebanon’s post-war security architecture ”, The New Arab , 12 July 2026; Lili Bayer, “ EU diplomatic service proposes mission to train Lebanese forces, documents show ”, Reuters, 24 June 2026;“ European Peace Facility: Council adopts EUR 100 million assistance measure in support of the Lebanese Armed Forces ”, press release, Council of the EU, 4 June 2026. Any new multinational mission would have no choice but to work alongside the Lebanese-Israeli-U.S. security arrangement, even if that is not fully defined. Any new multinational mission would have no choice but to work alongside the Lebanese-Israeli-U.S. security arrangement, even if that is not fully defined. States wishing to participate in a mission would almost certainly demand Security Council authorisation prior to sending troops to southern Lebanon so as to guarantee their legal and political protection. Given U.S. veto power, Washington’s support on the Council remains indispensable, meaning that UN members cannot circumvent the trilateral mechanism championed by the Trump administration. Between now and the end of December, diplomats should monitor the evolution of security arrangements on the ground in southern Lebanon, while seeking to work out with Washington what kind of international deployment, if any, would be beneficial to Lebanon and its stability. It is unlikely that any security arrangement, whether the June framework agreement and/or some future deal, will either fully disarm Hizbollah or completely dissuade Israel from conducting military operations in Lebanon. But withdrawing UNIFIL, with no immediate successor in place, could leave a vacuum that makes an already tense situation even more volatile. By inheriting UNIFIL’s most valuable functions – in particular, monitoring and on-the-ground deconfliction – a new multinational mission could set up a guardrail against fresh escalation. Ideally, that force would eventually assume other roles in bolstering a sustainable security arrangement for southern Lebanon that becomes durable enough to stand on its own feet. 2. Adapting the UN’s political strategy for Sudan The UN continues to be on the margins of diplomacy aimed at halting Sudan’s devastating civil war. Secretary-General Guterres’ appointment of Pekka Haavisto as the new UN envoy in February has offered the organisation an opportunity to refresh its approach. Ramtane Lamamra – the UN’s previous diplomatic lead – struggled to find a bridge between the main warring parties, the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), or to coordinate the array of mediators working to resolve the conflict. The UN has had varying degrees of success in securing local deals over aid access, and it continues to prepare for a possible role in overseeing aspects of a mooted ceasefire. 64 See the Sudan entry in Crisis Group Briefing, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , op. cit. It is hard to see the UN leading efforts to stop the war, given the number of powerful foreign states backing the belligerents, but it should use the coming months to support other diplomatic tracks and raise global awareness of the urgent need to end the fighting. 65 “ Sudan: Closed Consultations ”, Security Council Report, 17 April 2026. Nearly eighteen months ago, UN officials acknowledged that Sudan’s plight had become the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe. 66 “ UN Sudan Annual Results Report 2024 ”, UN Sudan, 4 June 2025. Conditions have only deteriorated since then. An independent UN panel determined that mass killings, rapes and other atrocities committed by the RSF in October 2025 in El Fasher, Darfur – the city that hosted the headquarters of the former UN peacekeeping operation UNAMID – were “indicators of a genocidal path”. 67 “ Sudan: Hallmarks of Genocide in El Fasher - Report of the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), UN Doc A/HRC/61/77, 19 February 2026. Diplomats and UN officials alike are sounding the alarm about similar risks in El-Obeid, North Kordofan. 68 “ Sudan: Imminent offensive on El Obeid must be halted – Türk warns of catastrophic impact on civilians ”, press release, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, 18 June 2026; “ Joint Statement of G7 Foreign Ministers on El Obeid, Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, July 2026; “ Security Council Press Statement on Sudan (SC/16392) ”, UN Security Council, 20 June 2026. The two warring sides and their outside backers still believe there is more to gain from fighting than from negotiations. As matters stand, the country is in effect partitioned between the army and the RSF. 69 Crisis Group Africa Report N°211, Divided Sudan, Elusive Peace , 13 April 2026. To date, political negotiations have yielded few results. Much of the diplomatic focus has fallen on the Quad, a platform involving the U.S. and the three Arab powers with the most sway over the conflict parties – Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Its September 2025 roadmap, however, has won over neither belligerent, while Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, at loggerheads in conflict settings from Libya to Yemen, are doubling down on backing the army and RSF, respectively, stymying agreement within the Quad about what to do. 70 “ Joint Statement on Restoring Peace and Security in Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, 12 September 2025; Comfort Ero and Alan Boswell, “ Latest Sudan Conference Shows Diplomacy is Backsliding ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 17 April 2026. In parallel, the UN is working alongside the African Union (AU), the EU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), a Horn of Africa body, and the Arab League to support Sudanese-led civilian political dialogues as part of a nascent diplomatic track called the Quintet; these mediators convened a meeting in Berlin in April and another in Addis Ababa two months later. 71 “ Sudan: Quintet Joint Statement on de-escalation of the conflict in Sudan ”, European External Action Service, 11 February 2026; “ Quintet Statement on Ongoing Consultations with Sudanese Political Actors ”, African Union, 6 June 2026. Sudanese participants cannot agree on how to move forward with the talks, however. Having completed an initial tour of Sudan and the region, Haavisto can begin revising the UN’s diplomatic strategy. 72 “ Pekka Haavisto (Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan) on the situation in the country – Press Conference ”, Office of the UN Spokesperson, 25 June 2026. He will need to reassure all parties that the UN will be an independent, impartial counterpart, even though the army-led government is the legally recognised one in New York. Haavisto needs to build rapport with others across Sudan’s fragmented political spectrum, including armed, political and civil players that are enlisted in the war, on one side or the other, or are non-aligned, as well as the various African, Arab and other countries directly involved in the conflict in one way or another. He will also need to reach out to the RSF, even if its deeds have earned it widespread and deserved condemnation. Lamamra struggled to maintain this balance, with critics seeing him as weighting his engagements too heavily toward the army-led authorities and its allies. 73 Crisis Group interviews, opposition political figures; RSF officials and allies, October-November 2025. Haavisto now has a chance for a reset. Haavisto should also strengthen the UN’s contributions within the Quintet. He could begin by stepping up outreach to various civilian groups between official Quintet meetings, with a view to mending fences between them. He could also help institute more consistent interactions between the Quintet and the army-led government, which has so far proven reluctant to get involved with a political process that is independent of its authority and takes place outside the country. 74 “ Quintet Statement Ahead of Visit to Khartoum, the Republic of Sudan, 8-10 September ”, Delegation of the European Union to the African Union, 8 September 2026. The army is instead pursuing its own “national dialogue” inside Sudan, which few of its political or armed opponents look likely to join. Behind the scenes, the UN should ... search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts [in Sudan]. Behind the scenes, the UN should also search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts, neither of which appears to have momentum at present. One way forward would be for Haavisto to work closely with counterparts to quietly float proposals for how Sudan could be governed whenever the main belligerents and their outside patrons summon the political will to seek an end to the war. Haavisto could help communicate these proposals to Quad and Quintet members, the two warring parties, and Sudan’s other main political movements and figures. Though it is hard to imagine a breakthrough any time soon given the entrenched positions on both sides, the UN should separately continue planning for a possible role in backing humanitarian access and ceasefire arrangements between the army and RSF should regional support for peace efforts eventually rise. 75 The UN is not formal member of the Quad, but it has worked informally with the U.S. to scope out technicalities of a monitoring mechanism for the prospective humanitarian truce that was outlined in the Quad’s September 2025 roadmap. Lastly, the UN can redouble its efforts to draw world attention to Sudan’s war and humanitarian disaster, if nothing else to caution states about possible spillover. The next Secretary-General should make this task a priority – including by paying a solidarity visit to refugee camps in countries neighbouring Sudan – and also warn of the mounting risks to states in the Horn and Red Sea regions should the conflict fester. 76 Alan Boswell, “ As the Horn of Africa Nears Boiling Point, Time for Urgent Diplomacy ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 17 July 2026. The UN’s new leader should ensure that Haavisto and other UN envoys covering the Horn, central Africa and the Middle East remain in close contact in the hope of identifying opportunities to break the diplomatic deadlock among states in these areas. 3. Encouraging a role for the General Assembly in Gaza’s ceasefire Having repeatedly called for a ceasefire to halt Israel’s campaign against Hamas in Gaza from 2023-2025, the General Assembly has devoted little energy to discussing whether the mechanisms created to uphold it are working. The Security Council’s November 2025 endorsement of the Trump administration’s ceasefire plan in Resolution 2803 – including its highly unusual authorisation of a Trump-chaired Board of Peace to serve as Gaza’s transitional administration – has erected a de-facto firewall between the UN and the diplomatic apparatus overseeing the Palestinian enclave’s future, at least until the Board’s UN mandate expires at the end of 2027. 77 “Resolution 2803”, op. cit. With Gaza’s reconstruction at a virtual standstill and Israel tightening its grip on the territory, UN member states risk sitting idle as the U.S.-dominated Board veers further off course. 78 Crisis Group Middle East Report N°257, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , 24 August 2026. The Board’s backtracking on the terms of its own fifteen-point roadmap – which features a scheme for decommissioning Hamas’s weapons agreed to by Palestinian factions but opposed by Israel – is just one of many troubling developments. The Security Council is, unfortunately, unlikely to consider corrective action until the Board mandate’s 2027 sunset. In the interim, member states should at a minimum use the General Assembly to assess the Board’s performance and to catalyse diplomatic pressure for putting Gaza on track toward recovery and Palestinian statehood. The General Assembly was the hub of UN diplomatic activity on Gaza throughout the war, as both President Joe Biden and President Trump blocked the Security Council from taking meaningful action. UN members convened the Assembly’s Emergency Special Session on the Occupied Palestinian Territories (its dedicated format for discussing the broader conflict) on eight separate occasions, and they debated five failed Security Council resolutions. 79 The General Assembly debated the nine vetoed resolutions under a Liechtenstein-led veto initiative, established by the General Assembly in April 2022. For full list of General Assembly meetings convened under the veto initiative, see “ Living with the Veto ”, Security Council Report, 23 March 2026, p. 8. Member states adopted five major General Assembly decisions on various aspects of the conflict, including the New York Declaration of September 2025, which bolstered recognition of Palestinian statehood. 80 “ Admission of new Members to the United Nations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/23, 10 May 2024; Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/24, 19 September 2024; “ Support for the mandate of the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/25, 16 December 2024; “ Protection of civilians and upholding legal and humanitarian obligations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/27, 13 June 2025; “ Endorsement of the New York Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine and the Implementation of the Two-State Solution ”, UNGA A/80/L.1/Rev.1, 10 September 2025. Though these measures had limited impact on the ground, they signalled growing international opposition to the war’s trajectory. The Security Council’s endorsement of Trump’s ceasefire plan upended these dynamics. By agreeing to the U.S.-drafted resolution (unenthusiastically supported by regional mediators and the State of Palestine), they in effect outsourced all responsibility for Gaza’s recovery and governance to the Board of Peace. 81 In Resolution 2803, the Security Council authorises the Board of Peace to set up a transitional administration (supervising a Palestinian technocratic committee, as well as matters including reconstruction of Gaza, public services, humanitarian assistance, movement of persons in and out of the strip and the envisioned International Stabilisation Force. “Resolution 2803”, op. cit.; Forti, Gowan and Rodenbeck, “What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council”, op. cit. Since then, the UN has been further isolated from diplomacy on Gaza. It neither participates in any of the Board’s structures nor has it been asked to help stand up the International Stabilisation Force envisaged by the Council-approved Trump plan. 82 Sigrid Kaag, who was the former UN Gaza Humanitarian Coordinator and the former UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, is a member of the Board of Peace’s Gaza Executive Board. The Board’s High Representative Nickolay Mladenov (a former UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process) has briefed the Council and submitted a report (as required by Resolution 2803), but the General Assembly has discussed the situation only once – indirectly – since November 2025. No member state has asked to reconvene the Emergency Special Session despite worsening conditions under the tenuous truce. 83 General Assembly Annual Event of the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People Commemorating the Nakba, 15 May 2026. The inattention seems particularly negligent given that Gaza’s circumstances are diverging from not only Resolution 2803, but also the array of General Assembly resolutions and international legal orders about Palestine. 84 Crisis Group Report, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , op. cit. The lack of tangible progress in nearly a year after reaching a purported ceasefire makes international actors complicit in a brutal status quo: Gaza’s people are in effect hostage to diplomatic forces outside their control. Unless something changes, they will remain under siege, subject to bombardment and denied a future until the Board of Peace decides that Hamas has met Israel’s demands. Washington would likely veto any Security Council action perceived to criticise Israel – which receives unconditional backing from the U.S. at the UN – or to cast doubt on the legitimacy and efficacy of Trump’s peace efforts. But that ought not to be a justification for inaction in the General Assembly or elsewhere. UN members should use the General Assembly to challenge the Board of Peace’s unhelpful domination of the diplomatic space. UN members should use the General Assembly to challenge the Board of Peace’s unhelpful domination of the diplomatic space. The next meeting of the Global Alliance for the Two-State Solution, scheduled for September, could kickstart that endeavour. Member states should also consider reconvening the General Assembly’s Tenth Emergency Special Session to continue these efforts beyond High-Level Week. In addition, members should use these forums to offer political backing to the Palestinian technocratic committee as a means of asserting Palestinian ownership of reconstruction. These platforms provide an opportunity to reaffirm the necessity of the UN-led aid distribution network in Gaza, which remains the most capable one in the strip. Members might also signal the costs they would impose on Israel (bilaterally or in regional blocs) if it continues to obstruct provisions of the ceasefire and prevent the Palestinian technocratic committee from working in Gaza. 85 For example, on 8 September the British foreign secretary announced a raft of measures against Israel responding to its construction of illegal settlements in the West Bank and obstruction of the Trump ceasefire plan for Gaza. See Ed Miliband, “ Foreign Secretary Oral Statement on Israel-Palestine ”, speech to UK Parliament, 8 September 2026. For background, see Crisis Group Report, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , op. cit. States should also consider tasking the Secretariat with preparing a report to evaluate follow-through on the New York Declaration, adopted a year ago, by the beginning of the 82nd General Assembly session in September 2027. The Declaration commits its signatories to a range of measures to end the war in Gaza, to facilitate a credible pathway toward Palestinian self-determination and to support a sovereign Palestinian state living peacefully alongside Israel. 86 “ Endorsement of the New York Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine and the Implementation of the Two-State Solution ”, op. cit. Such a report could be useful as the Council considers whether to renew the Board of Peace’s mandate, which it must do by 31 December 2027. Member states could ask the Secretary-General to focus on whether the Board is advancing commitments to reduce civilian suffering, rehabilitate Gaza and preserve a viable political horizon – and whether it is acting consistent with Security Council, General Assembly and International Court of Justice interventions on these matters. While UN members cannot circumvent the deeply flawed ceasefire plan altogether, they can work through the world body to keep a global spotlight on Gaza. It is past time for the General Assembly to recover a sense of urgency for mobilising diplomatic pressure in support of the ceasefire and keeping space open for the Palestinians to pursue self-determination. 4. Reinforcing security and justice support to Haiti International efforts to help restore security in Haiti have reached a decisive phase. The Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a multilateral mission authorised by the Security Council in September 2025 and backed with UN logistical support, landed in Haiti in June. 87 “ Resolution 2793 ”, UNSC S/RES/2793, 30 September 2025. Expected to be at full strength by the end of the year, the force faces the daunting task of confronting armed gangs that have held much of the country hostage for years. 88 Crisis Group Report, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , op. cit.; “ Situation of human rights in Haiti ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights A/HRC/61/74, 23 March 2026. International efforts to staff, fund and equip the GSF are essential to ending this painful chapter in Haiti’s history. But even if this force puts gangs on the back foot, it will only be the start of a far longer campaign to bring peace to the country. Haiti’s government and international partners should work closely with the UN to build exit ramps for individuals willing to abandon the gangs and reinforce new judicial bodies to investigate and prosecute gang crimes. The GSF’s close working relationship with the UN could help it avoid the problems that plagued its predecessor, the Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support mission. A new UN support office services the force’s logistics needs (ranging from supplying rations and fuel to covering its medical services and constructing bases) and channels monetary contributions its way. 89 “ Budgets for the periods from 1 October 2025 to 30 June 2026 and from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027 for the United Nations Support Office in Haiti ”, UNGA A/80/630, 10 February 2026. Reasonably predictable funding from the UN’s assessed budget has enabled eight countries to pledge enough troops to surpass the initial target of 5,500 personnel, though as of publication only around 1,200 troops are on the ground. 90 As of publication, the GSF included personnel sent from Chad, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mongolia and Sri Lanka. A separate UN trust fund has nearly $226 million in voluntary donations, which have been promised to cover the wages of deployed personnel. 91 As of 30 June, the Trust Fund had $233 million in total pledges, with $184 million in cash receipts. The UN had spent approximately $67 million of the cash receipts leaving $117 million in hand. “ Contributions to the Trust Fund for the Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission for Haiti authorised under SCR 2699 (2023) and Gang Suppression Force (GSF) authorised under SCR 2793 ”, UN, 13 July 2026; “ United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti: Report of the Secretary-General ”, UNSC S/2026/574, 14 July 2026, p. 10. Informal ties also reinforce the force’s partnership with the UN. The Standing Group of Partners, the ad hoc political body with the job of overseeing the mission, appointed UN peacekeeping veterans to the force’s highest ranking civilian and uniformed positions. 92 The Standing Group of Partners includes the U.S., Canada, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Kenya, and the Bahamas. “ Special representative named for U.S. backed-Gang Suppression Force in Haiti ”, Miami Herald , 2 December 2025; “ UN-appointed anti-gang force commander arrives in Haiti to lead expanded mission ”, Haitian Times , 15 May 2026. These officials are coordinating with senior staff in BINUH, the UN political office in Haiti tasked with engaging Haitian counterparts on governance and human rights, and in the force’s logistics support office. The UN headquarters gave wide-ranging assistance to the force as it went about its technical preparations, including by helping prepare its concept of operations and carry out pre-deployment training. 93 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and UN officials, New York and Port-au-Prince, February, April and June 2026. Difficulties will inevitably arise once the GSF begins going after the gangs in earnest. Civilians are at risk of becoming collateral damage once the mission launches offensives. 94 The Multinational Security Support mission, by contrast, never mustered more than 1,000 police personnel, struggled to secure funding and battled the gangs only alongside the national police. Troop-contributing countries that have taken part in previous UN peacekeeping operations will need to ensure that the soldiers they send to Haiti are prepared for a hostile environment. The Standing Group of Partners and the Security Council should be vigilant in monitoring how the force polices its members’ conduct and metes out any necessary discipline, especially given the history of international personnel committing sexual abuses while serving in Haiti. 95 “ Citing unpunished sex abuse, rights groups urge halt to Sri Lankan troops Haiti deployment ”, The Miami Herald , 28 June 2026. Any gains will be short-lived if Haiti and its partners do not take steps to dismantle the criminal groups for good. Once the force reaches full capacity, member states hope that it can quickly impose a modicum of security. 96 Crisis Group Report, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , op. cit. But any gains will be short-lived if Haiti and its partners do not take steps to dismantle the criminal groups for good. Offering individuals the opportunity to leave the gangs safely, with support for new livelihoods through a program of disarmament, dismantlement and reintegration, will be critical for winding down these groups. 97 The Haitian government and the UN do not use the more common term “demobilisation”, which refers to dissolving non-state armed groups as defined under international humanitarian law. Instead, they refer to “dismantlement”, which envisages individual rather than collective action. “ Letter dated 29 May 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/449, 29 May 2026, p. 3. Important steps have already been taken to this effect. First, in early 2026 Haitian authorities reactivated the National Commission for Disarmament, Dismantlement and Reintegration, which the UN has offered to support in a range of ways. 98 “ Letter dated 29 May 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/449, 29 May 2026. Secondly, the Security Council revised BINUH’s mandate in January to include assisting the state in designing and running a program to find exit ramps for gang members. 99 “ Resolution 2814 ”, UNSC S/RES/2814, 29 January 2026. The UN is also providing technical support to newly established special judicial units, mandated to address complex corruption cases and serious human rights violations, which will also be indispensable to any long-term campaign to weaken the gangs. The hope is that these courts will be able to address the links between powerful actors and criminal activity that have long gone unpunished. The government is working toward providing stronger security protection for the judges taking on these cases, as in the past many have recused themselves after being threatened. 100 In May, the Haitian government launched two specialised judicial units to investigate and prosecute mass crimes, sexual violence and financial crimes, with technical support from the Office of the High Commissioner of Human Rights and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. These units, which are expected to start work soon, could help bring to justice the main perpetrators of crimes committed by gangs, as well as their main supporters. “ United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti: Report of the Secretary-General ”, op. cit., p. 5; Crisis Group telephone interviews, Haitian government and UN officials, July 2025. The focus of the Haitian authorities and their foreign counterparts, understandably, is on combating the gangs by force. But they should simultaneously lay the groundwork for dismantlement that is robust enough to ensure former members are not drawn back into the gangs’ orbit, whether by poverty or the weakness of local security forces. The UN should make sure these long-term objectives do not get lost in the push for tactical victories, particularly because they will require considerably more funding than is now available. 101 Estimates of the needs range from $13.5 million for minimal assistance to over $150 million for a comprehensive suite of DDR and judicial sector programs. “ Letter dated 29 May 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, op. cit. For that reason, donor countries should not just fund the multinational force but also include both dismantlement projects and justice reform in their support to the country. 102 Canadian-French support for establishing two specialised justice units is a model worth replicating. “ Specialised Judicial Units in Haiti ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, June 2026. In May, the Secretary-General presented to the Security Council several options for backing disarmament, dismantlement and reintegration initiatives and strengthening Haiti’s judicial system. UN member states have yet to weigh in on which of these options they would be willing to help fund. “ Letter dated 29 May 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, op. cit. 5. Preserving UN operations in the Central African Republic UN peacekeepers have been at the forefront of international efforts to protect civilians and back peace initiatives in the Central African Republic (CAR) since first being dispatched to the country in 2014. The U.S. and China, two of the Council’s permanent members, have suggested that the mission, known as MINUSCA, should now begin preparing to exit, citing the progress the country has made toward stability. (Their own interest is to lower the cost of UN peacekeeping.) Elections held in late December 2025 without a major disruption may bolster their case. 103 Charles Bouëssel, “ Central African Republic: Consolidating Security Gains after the Elections ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 27 January 2026. But when renewing MINUSCA’s mandate in November, diplomats should ensure that the mission retains sufficient capacity to protect civilians and deter armed groups in the country’s troubled east, since it is the only entity that can provide a buffer against worsening instability in that region. MINUSCA continues to fill gaps that the Central African authorities cannot plug. A guarantor of the 2019 peace agreement, the UN mission oversees local peace dialogues and disarmament programs across the country. 104 The Union for Peace in the Central African Republic, Return, Reclamation and Rehabilitation and the Patriotic Movement for the Central African Republic are the most prominent armed groups participating in these disarmament programs. See: “ The Situation in the Central African Republic ”, UNSC S/2026/494, 15 June 2026, paras 8-10. Though CAR’s allies – Rwanda and Russian paramilitaries from the Wagner Group – helped Bangui regain control of towns across the country after a 2021 rebel offensive, MINUSCA is the only external partner tasked with protecting civilians from violence. In many areas outside the capital Bangui, local institutions depend on the mission to build and repair government offices, supply logistical assistance and offer physical protection. The threat of insurgency in CAR is much lower than it was a few years ago, but pockets of insecurity persist along the country’s eastern borders. 105 Bouëssel, “ Central African Republic: Consolidating Security Gains after the Elections ”, op. cit. Fighters from the ex-Séléka rebel coalition, which seized power in 2013 and plunged the country into civil war, as well as allied militias are active in the north east, most recently attacking CAR state forces and UN peacekeepers on 30 June in Am-Dafock, on the Sudan border. 106 “ Central African Republic Situation Report No. 74 as of 30 June, 2026 ”, UN OCHA, 2 July 2026; “ MINUSCA strongly condemns the attack against Am Dafock and the firing targeting the Mission’s base ”, press release, UN OCHA, 30 June 2026. Separately, the Zandé self-defence militia based in Haut-Mbomou prefecture, in the south east, continue to assail civilians and state forces. 107 Crisis Group Africa Report N°319, Central African Republic: Reining in the Zandé Militia , 20 November 2025. UN peacekeepers are often the only force capable of deterring or responding to urgent threats [in the Central African Republic]. Intercommunal violence, opportunistic crime and conflicts between nomadic herders and sedentary farmers remain prevalent nationwide. 108 Crisis Group Africa Report N°317, Violence and Herding in the Central African Republic: Time to Act , 28 May 2025. Women and girls are vulnerable to rape in many places as a result. Spillover from Sudan’s civil war exacerbates these risks: Central African rebels have become war entrepreneurs, providing fighters for both the RSF and the Sudanese army in exchange for money, while over 40,000 Sudanese refugees have fled into north-eastern CAR. UN peacekeepers are often the only force capable of deterring or responding to urgent threats. These developments should give Council members pause when they are considering a drawdown for MINUSCA. In November 2025, the U.S. pushed the Council to task the mission with charting an exit strategy ahead of the mandate renewal, owing in part to their assessment of CAR’s improved conditions and their scepticism about renewing UN operations indefinitely. 109 A draft is expected to be circulated by 15 September. “ Resolution 2800 ”, UNSC S/RES/2800, para 48; “ Central African Republic: Vote on MINUSCA’s Mandate Renewal ”, Security Council Report, 12 November 2025. U.S. and Chinese diplomats have found common cause in lobbying for reductions to the mission’s budget. 110 Crisis Group interviews, UN diplomats, New York, November 2025. See also UN Security Council, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10,041st Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10041, 13 November 2025; “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10,111st Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10041, 25 February 2026; and UN Security Council, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10,181st Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10181, 23 June 2026. Separately, the UN’s liquidity crisis has already forced the mission to repatriate nearly 4,000 troops (more than one quarter of the total) and close 21 operating bases that allowed MINUSCA to intervene in a range of conflict-affected areas outside Bangui. 111 UN leaders used the financial constraints as motivation to reposition MINUSCA personnel in a more mobile posture to get the most out of the smaller footprint. Crisis Group interviews, UN officials, July 2026. Some of the temporary bases had been set up to support the UN’s election assistance to CAR. “ Report of the Secretary-General on the Central African Republic ”, UNSC S/2026/494, 15 June 2026. Though the UN’s financial crisis will make it hard to restore MINUSCA to its mandated strength, Council members should make sure that debates about the mission’s long-term future do not undermine its ability to consolidate the country’s security gains in the short term. In line with the November 2025 resolution, the Central African government and MINUSCA have begun work on a transition plan. A confidential report envisages MINUSCA shifting to a role of strategic support, with some state authority tasks transferable in the short and medium term, while others (notably protection of civilians) remain non-transferable. It also highlights major budgetary challenges Bangui faces in meeting these responsibilities. Diplomats should use the mandate renewal to draw an explicit link between rising insecurity on CAR’s eastern borders, making sure that the mission retains sufficient capacity to conduct operations in that part of the country. They should also encourage MINUSCA to make non-military efforts to prevent further escalation through local political dialogues followed by various forms of disarmament. Council members should ensure that MINUSCA’s leadership is working closely with UN envoys in the Horn of Africa to better anticipate and react to any spillover from Sudan’s war. All Security Council members acknowledge MINUSCA’s importance in helping CAR achieve a degree of stability through protecting civilians, restoring public services and supporting political dialogue, even if they continue to debate when and how those parts of its work should be whittled down. For the moment, the Council should help CAR consolidate gains rather than push for a hasty downsizing that would generate risks in a country where the UN has already invested heavily for the past decade. 6. Rallying around the International Criminal Court The Trump administration’s “sweeping campaign” to dismantle the International Criminal Court (ICC), announced in July, is the latest salvo in its assault upon the international order. 112 The campaign reportedly includes highlighting the court’s harms through high-level diplomatic outreach, threats to revisit U.S. assistance if states do not reject the Court’s ability to prosecute U.S. officials, visa revocations, travel bans and additional sanctions on ICC personnel. “ State Department Launches Campaign to Dismantle International Criminal Court’s Threat to American Sovereignty ”, U.S. Department of State, 13 July 2026; Victor Jack, “ US pressures NATO allies to destroy International Criminal Court ”, Politico , 9 September 2026. It is not the first time that the U.S. has openly clashed with the ICC or sanctioned its personnel. 113 As of publication, “nine of the eighteen Judges, both of the two Deputy-Prosecutors, the former Prosecutor and one staff member have been sanctioned by the United States”. See “ The ICC strongly rejects new US sanctions designations ”, press release, International Criminal Court, 19 August 2026. But its latest move to obstruct the Court’s work by sanctioning its president and threatening its member state backers is a regrettable escalation that risks setting a precedent for U.S. efforts to bend other parts of the multilateral system to its will. A number of the UN’s most powerful member states (including the U.S., Russia and China) never joined the Court and generally resist its efforts in situations where they have deemed interests, member states that do back the court can chart their own course. Those that have not already done so should make clear their continued support for a strong, independent ICC, noting its role as the only permanent tribunal mandated to pursue individual accountability for international crimes, including those linked to conflict. The current schism between the U.S. and the ICC is the latest episode in what has been a rollercoaster relationship. 114 Stephen Pomper, “ The International Criminal Court’s Case against the United States in Afghanistan ”, Just Security , 13 November 2017. The U.S. never ratified the Rome Statute – the treaty establishing the ICC – even though it played a central role in negotiating the text and signed the document. Washington has long worried that the Court would prosecute U.S. servicemembers for their conduct abroad. In the early years of the Court, the George W. Bush administration purported to “un-sign” the treaty and pressured ICC member states to pledge they would not hand over U.S. personnel to the Court. Though the U.S. later cooperated closely with the ICC in some matters, the prosecutor’s decision in 2017 to investigate the conduct of international forces deployed to Afghanistan prompted the first Trump White House to place certain Court officers under sanctions. 115 For example, the Bush and Barack Obama administrations supported cases involving situations in the DRC and Sudan, and the Biden administration provided evidence to the Court regarding alleged Russian war crimes in Ukraine. Stephen Pomper, “ The US and ICC May Still Steer Past Each Other – Why and How ”, Just Security , 5 April 2018. The Biden administration lifted those, several months before the ICC prosecutor announced that he would “deprioritise” work in Afghanistan that was unrelated to the Taliban. 116 Nahal Toosi, “ Biden lifts sanctions on International Criminal Court officials ”, Politico , 2 April 2021; “ Statement of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, Karim A. A. Khan QC, following the application for an expedited order under article 18(2) seeking authorisation to resume investigations in the Situation in Afghanistan ”, press release, International Criminal Court, 27 September 2021. For a brief moment, even some of the ICC’s staunchest critics in the U.S. Congress lined up behind its work on Russia’s war in Ukraine, applauding its indictment of Russian President Vladimir Putin, among others. 117 Bipartisan letter from U.S. senators to U.S. President Joseph Biden , 24 March 2023; “ House Resolution Supports ICC Arrest Warrant for Putin & Lvova-Belova ”, press release, Office of Congressman Mike Quigley, 18 April 2023; Bipartisan letter from U.S. congressional representatives to U.S. President Joseph Biden , 6 June 2023. But relations soured again when the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli leaders Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant in late 2024 and have only gotten worse since the second Trump administration came into office. 118 Brian Finucane, Stephen Pomper, and Mairav Zonszein, “ All Eyes on The Hague: The ICC Prosecutor’s Move against Hamas and Israeli Leader s”, Crisis Group Commentary, 24 May 2024. The latter imposed a fresh wave of sanctions on several Court officials in February 2025. 119 “ Imposing Sanctions on the International Criminal Court ”, White House, 6 February 2025. Trump has allowed that this new campaign is in part an effort to defend his political allies in Israel. 120 “ TRANSCRIPT: President Trump Holds a Cabinet Meeting at Camp David, 7.31.26 ”, Senate Democrats, 31 July 2026. Concerns about the Court’s future come during a period when respect for legal restraints on the use of force is wilting. 121 Stewart Patrick, “ What’s Driving the Trump Administration’s Push to Dismantle the ICC? ”, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 15 July 2026. Many states are demonstrating brazen disregard for international humanitarian law. 122 Mirjana Spoljaric, “ Speech given by the International Committee of the Red Cross at the UN Security Council Open Debate on the Protection of Civilians in Armed Conflict ”, New York, 20 May 2026. The Court has struggled to counter this trend. Even with 125 member states, its leverage is limited, particularly when big non-member state powers are implicated in alleged crimes that fall under its jurisdiction. The Security Council, which has the authority to refer cases to the ICC, has done so only twice – in Darfur (2005) and Libya (2o11) – a reflection of its divided geopolitical backing. Some Court watchers point to its institutional failings, including lengthy procedures and a number of prominent failed prosecutions. Sexual abuse allegations against former prosecutor Karim Khan (which he has denied) led to his dismissal from office at the end of July and dented the Court’s legitimacy. 123 “ Independent Expert Review of the International Criminal Court and the Rome Statute System – Final Report ”, 30 September 2020; John B Bellinger III, “ The ICC Has Real Flaws. Dismantling It Without an Alternative Is Not the Answer ”, Council on Foreign Relations, 16 July 2026. But there are limits to what the ICC can achieve without strong political backing, as it depends on member states and the Security Council to enforce its judgments. 124 For example, South Africa (a state party of the Rome Statute) failed to enforce the ICC arrest warrant for former Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir when he visited South Africa in June 2015, while Mongolia hosted Russian President Putin for a state visit in 2024. “ Al-Bashir case: ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II decides not to refer South Africa’s non-cooperation to the ASP or the UNSC ”, press release, International Criminal Court, 6 July 2017; Stephen Pomper, “ Assessing the ICC’s Impact in Ukraine ”, Just Security , 6 February 2026. Unfortunately, Washington’s campaign has resonated with other states who are now looking to abandon their commitments under the Rome Statute. At the end of June, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger formally initiated their withdrawal from the ICC, calling it an “instrument of neocolonial oppression in the hands of imperialism”. 125 “ JOINT COMMUNIQUE OF THE STATES OF THE AES CONFEDERATION RELATING TO THE WITHDRAWAL FROM THE ROME STATUTE OF THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT ”, The African Centre for Democracy and Human Rights Studies, September 2025. Whatever the ideological justification, leaving the Court also has the practical benefit of shielding these regimes and their Russian partners from international accountability for acts committed once withdrawal becomes effective (which takes place after a year’s delay). Even though the three states were motivated primarily by parochial interests, the Trump campaign can only have made it politically easier for them to make this move. 126 Tweet by U.S. State Department Bureau of African Affairs, @AsstSecStateAf, Bureau of African Affairs, 2:21 pm, 17 July 2026. Other states have been more clearly motivated by desire to improve relations with Washington. Though the ICC has been investigating the situation in Venezuela since 2018, Caracas only submitted its withdrawal papers to the UN in July, after the U.S. announced its campaign. The same month, Chad also announced its withdrawal from the ICC, citing bias against Africa and the Court’s limited effectiveness. With little risk of domestic backlash, President Mahamat Déby may be seeking to bolster U.S. support for joint counter-terrorism operations in the Lake Chad basin and for Chadian troops deployed to the GSF in Haiti. 127 Crisis Group, “On Our Radar – Chad”, 7 August 2026. Colombia’s new president looks to be mulling withdrawal from the Court as part of an effort to move closer to the U.S. and discredit his country’s own ICC-backed transitional justice court, which was created by a 2016 peace agreement with former rebel fighters. 128 Lucía Martínez, “ Colombia ICC withdrawal: Reports say Bogotá may quit the war crimes court ”, Rio Times , 18 August 2026. While the Court’s critics tend to disparage it as feckless, it serves an important function in reinforcing and applying international legal rules relating to mass violence. While the Court’s critics tend to disparage it as feckless, it serves an important function in reinforcing and applying international legal rules relating to mass violence. It keeps the prospect of accountability on the table even in situations where the ability to enforce its decisions is limited. 129 Crisis Group Briefing, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Security , op. cit. Its diminution is likely to erode the force of international humanitarian law yet further. The Court’s member states should work together to limit the damage. While they may not be the world’s most powerful, there is strength in their numbers. They should encourage states that are vulnerable to U.S. pressure to stay the course and do what they can to buttress the Court’s resiliency. At a practical level, countries could offer basic banking services to ICC officials who have been targeted by U.S. sanctions. Member states should also use their negotiations of the annual General Assembly resolution on the ICC, scheduled to take place between October and November, to drum up public support for its work and galvanise pushback against the U.S. attack on this pillar of the international justice architecture. 7. Recalibrating UN operations in Myanmar Myanmar’s installation of a nominally civilian administration in April, following elections stage-managed by the military four months earlier, has created a dilemma for the UN. The elections have not restored state authority or legitimacy, and Naypyitaw does not have a credible strategy for ending the country’s armed conflict, either through negotiation or military victory. 130 Crisis Group Asia Briefing N°188, Myanmar’s New Administration: Military Consolidation, Not Transition , 3 June 2026. Humanitarian conditions continue to deteriorate as fighting, economic decline and fear of conscription grip the country. 131 “ Myanmar Humanitarian Update no. 51 ”, UN OCHA, 9 March 2026. Even so, more of Myanmar’s regional neighbours are giving the new administration de facto recognition, with Min Aung Hlaing – the coup leader who is now president – recently visiting India, China, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. Beijing maintains a firm position limiting discussion of Myanmar at the UN, while Secretary-General Guterres has shown little willingness to invest political capital in the issue. Absent new diplomatic momentum in the near term, UN officials will need to calibrate engagement carefully to reduce harm, sustain livelihoods and support development without conferring legitimacy on abusive forms of rule. Much of this work will fall to the new UN leadership in Yangon. In October 2025, Guterres appointed veteran official Gwyn Lewis as resident and humanitarian coordinator ad interim, ending the ineffective practice of rotating the position among agency heads. 132 Lewis has the ad interim designation because the Secretary-General does not want to acknowledge the authorities politically by writing to seek their agreement to the appointment. See Crisis Group Special Briefing N°12, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2024-2025 , 10 September 2024. The resident coordinator will need to shape the UN’s engagement with the new administration while ensuring the organisation can continue delivering essential humanitarian and development assistance. Just as importantly, the office should provide clear strategic direction to the whole UN country team so that agencies operate according to a consistent approach within current political constraints. UN officials will also need to manage relations with Myanmar’s ethnic armed groups. Aid agencies already deliver assistance in parts of the country outside state control, working through local partners despite the absence of formal agreements with Naypyitaw. As the devastating March 2025 earthquake showed, the UN remains one of the few organisations capable of delivering international aid at scale to civilians in much of the country, including areas outside government control. 133 Richard Horsey, “ Support Vital for Myanmar’s Quake Victims, Despite Military Obstacles ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 1 April 2025; “ End of Mission Report United Nations Disaster Assessment & Coordination – Earthquake 7.7M Response – Myanmar (29Mar-16Apr 2025) ”, UN OCHA, 23 February 2026; “ First person: Myanmar aid workers brave conflict and harsh conditions to bring aid to earthquake victims ”, UN, 30 April 2025. The World Bank and the Asian Development Bank have become the largest and most consistent providers of assistance to Myanmar’s people, but they rightly cannot channel funds through a government they do not recognise. Their support is therefore delivered off-budget – outside state systems – and depends on UN agencies for fiduciary oversight and distribution. The resident coordinator will need to mind the political sensitivities of the UN role in providing this support, as well as the differing approaches of neighbouring states – including Bangladesh, China, India and Thailand – toward informal cross-border assistance. 134 Thomas Kean, “ Time to Reset Bangladesh’s Approach to the Rohingya ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 8 July 2026; Crisis Group Asia Briefing N°186, Fractured Heartland: Shan Politics and Conflict in Post-coup Myanmar , 27 November 2025. The next Secretary-General will have an opportunity to reset the UN’s overall strategy [in Myanmar] and provide stronger political backing for the envoy. The same balancing act applies to the UN’s diplomatic track. Special Envoy Julie Bishop, who has struggled to translate her high-level regional access into meaningful entry points for UN diplomacy, has burned most of her bridges with Myanmar’s leaders by taking an increasingly strident public line – for example, returning from Naypyitaw to tell UN member states in June that the election was designed to entrench military rule and that Min Aung Hlaing’s proposed 100-day peace plan inspires no confidence. 135 “Special Envoy on Myanmar’s remarks to the General Assembly”, UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, 19 June 2026. The next Secretary-General will have an opportunity to reset the UN’s overall strategy and provide stronger political backing for the envoy. 136 The envoy role was mandated by the UN General Assembly in December 2017 to support UN engagement on a range of political priorities. “ Situation of human rights in Myanmar ”, UN General Assembly, UN Doc. A/RES/72/248, 23 January 2018. An important test will come at the UN General Assembly. Since the 2021 coup, China and the U.S. have informally maintained the status quo by leaving in place the incumbent ambassador, Kyaw Moe Tun, who was appointed by the elected government and later aligned himself with the parallel National Unity Government. Naypyitaw is expected to press its case to have its nominee recognised as Myanmar’s permanent representative when the Credentials Committee meets in November. China committed in a 17 June statement with Min Aung Hlaing in Beijing to support Myanmar’s “full, equal and constructive participation” at the UN, repeating this formula in the General Assembly two days later. 137 “ Joint Statement of the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the People’s Republic of China on Accelerating the Building of a China – Myanmar Community with a Shared Future (17 June 2026) ”, Republic of the Union of Myanmar, 18 June 2026; and informal meeting of the General Assembly plenary convened to hear the Special Envoy’s briefing on Myanmar, 19 June 2026. It is unclear what diplomatic capital Beijing may expend to this end. A decision has been put off each year because the permanent members who sit on the Credentials Committee – China, the U.S. and Russia – have preferred the status quo to a divisive vote, and because any consideration of the competing credentials for Myanmar could prompt a similar debate about the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan. 138 The Committee, appointed at the General Assembly’s first plenary meeting under rule 28, met once in the 80th session, on 25 November 2025. Its report proposed a single postponement of the competing credentials for both Myanmar and Afghanistan, adopted without a vote. See “Report of the Credentials Committee”, A/80/547, 25 November 2025, paras 8 to 10, approved by the General Assembly on 12 December 2025 (Resolution 80/114). The credentials debate could coincide with the International Court of Justice’s expected ruling in the genocide case against Myanmar that was filed by The Gambia. 139 Public hearings in The Gambia v. Myanmar case closed at the International Court of Justice on 29 January 2026, and judgment is pending. The Court will rule both on whether Myanmar committed genocide and on whether it failed to prevent and punish genocidal acts. A finding that Myanmar committed genocide would be the first time the Court has held a state responsible for such a crime. In the two previous genocide judgments, Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro and Croatia v. Serbia , the Court found a failure to prevent and punish in the first and no proven specific intent in the second. See “The concluding stage of The Gambia v. Myanmar genocide case before the International Court of Justice”, Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect, 10 February 2026. Although the case’s outcome remains uncertain, a finding of state responsibility arriving at the same time as a credentials dispute would intensify international divisions over the issue of the Myanmar administration’s legitimacy. It would also narrow even further the UN’s room for manoeuvre in Myanmar, since Naypyitaw would view it with even more antagonism. The cost for regional leaders of associating with Min Aung Hlaing might rise as well, complicating high-level visits to the country though probably not turning the tide on diplomatic normalisation. The UN does not have the leverage to achieve major change in Myanmar. But the organisation is crucial for delivering humanitarian and other support to vulnerable civilians. A credible operational strategy, backed by sustained political support from headquarters, will therefore remain essential to efforts to alleviate public hardship and the effects of armed conflict. 8. Protecting the UN’s gender work in conflict settings The UN’s reform agenda has raised thorny issues about how the institution should organise its work to support women and girls. In late 2025, Secretary-General Guterres proposed merging the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) with UN Women as part of the UN80 initiative. 140 Other proposed mergers under UN80 include combining the UN Development Programme and the UN Office for Project Services; the UN Institute for Training and Research and the UN System Staff College; and the World Health Organisation and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS. UNFPA leads the UN’s work on sexual and reproductive health, while UN Women (approximately one third the size of UNFPA) advocates for normative shifts on gender issues, including the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda, and distributes funding to NGOs for related programming. 141 With an annual budget of $1.53 billion, UNFPA’s model focuses on service delivery through 3,569 staff in 150 countries. “ As-Is Analysis: A Baseline for the UNFPA - UN Women Strategic Merger Assessment ”, UN80 Initiative, Work Package 4, Working Document, 6 March 2026. Whether the merger will come to pass is not clear. Amid aid cuts and pushback against gender equality worldwide, many member states and UN officials worry that combining these entities would hobble the UN’s work on gender, including efforts to support women and girls affected by conflict, for years to come. The Secretary-General’s proposal included a request for a UN-prepared report (published in March) that evaluated the risks and benefits of a merger – an idea that had been discussed and discarded in 2023. 142 Member states and UN officials report a sense that, whatever its findings, the study was meant to recommend a merger because the Secretary-General and Deputy Secretary-General wished to show that they were serious about making large-scale reforms to make the UN more efficient. For more, see “ Independent Review of the UN System’s Capacity to Deliver on Gender Equality ”, Dalberg, 11 February 2023. The merger it proposed would bring together UNFPA and UN Women in a new entity with a unified voice. It would also save the UN between $32 and $38 million per year, which the UN would urge member states to reinvest in the new entity’s work. 143 “ Preliminary Findings from the Strategic Merger Assessment of UNFPA and UN Women ”, UN80 Initiative, 30 March 2026. The assessment acknowledged, but did not suggest ways to mitigate, the risk that member states could eliminate important but contentious areas of work – including a number of sexual and reproductive health services and work on LGBTQI+ protections – during negotiations to create the new entity. 144 Given that the U.S. has been spearheading the pressure on the Secretary-General and his deputy to show their willingness to streamline the UN, combined with U.S. positions against the UN’s gender equality and WPS, many member states and UN officials point out that this merger proposal is like offering the U.S. a prime opportunity to weaken the UN’s gender work for years to come, by opening a negotiation on a new mandate where no negotiation or new mandate is necessary or desirable. [The] separate mandates [of UN Women and UNFPA] help the UN respond to distinct political, security and humanitarian issues. There are other risks, too. Though both agencies work on gender issues in conflict-affected countries, their separate mandates help the UN respond to distinct political, security and humanitarian issues. 145 In 2025, UNFPA was active in efforts to ameliorate 50 humanitarian crises, while in 2024 UN Women was working in 43. See “ 2026 Humanitarian Action Overview ”, UNFPA, April 2026; and “ Humanitarian Action Annual Report 2024”, UN Women, 2025. In Afghanistan, for example, UNFPA runs programs including menstrual health education and support for midwives, all in compliance with Taliban edicts. 146 “ Youth centre provides life-changing menstrual hygiene information and supplies to Afghan girls ”, UNFPA Afghanistan, 28 May 2026. Though interactions between the Taliban and UNFPA personnel are sometimes “tense”, the authorities recognise the need for the agency’s services. 147 Crisis Group interview, UN official, New York, July 2026. UN Women’s Afghanistan office is on shakier ground. The Taliban consider UN Women to be among their loudest critics and reject the agency’s frequent calls for repealing highly restrictive decrees as interference in Afghanistan’s internal affairs. 148 Mohammad Farshad Daryosh, “ Potzel criticizes bans on women, girls in Afghanistan ”, Tolo News, 8 March 2023; “ IEA-MOFA statement regarding SRSG briefing to UNSC ”, press release, 22 June 2023. While UN Women supports livelihood projects that the Taliban see as consistent with their goals of keeping the economy afloat and help the agency maintain an in-country presence, its normative positions are a persistent source of friction. Combining the two UN entities may have the effect of imputing these positions to UNFPA and create unnecessary risks for the latter. 149 “ Empowering Afghan Women and Energizing Economies ”, UN Women Afghanistan, 2025. UN efforts to support more than one million Rohingya refugees from Myanmar living in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, also show why keeping UN Women and UNFPA separate is helpful in providing support for women and girls affected by conflict. 150 Kean, “ Time to Reset Bangladesh’s Approach to the Rohingya ”, op. cit. UNFPA offers health services in response to prevalent sexual violence and high pregnancy rates. It must be politically adroit in its engagement with Bangladeshi authorities, given local sensitivities around sexual and reproductive health. 151 Crisis Group telephone interview, humanitarian health practitioner, 25 June 2024. See also Cristal Downing, “ Amid Aid Cuts, a Renewed U.S. Policy Increases Health Risks for Women and Girls in Conflict Areas ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 3 March 2025. By contrast, UN Women supports women refugees (including through vocational training) and is involved in politically complex conversations with Dhaka about supporting eventual refugee return to Myanmar. 152 Kean, “ Time to Reset Bangladesh’s Approach to the Rohingya ”, op. cit. Currently, the conversations about health care and political matters are separate, so if the two need to raise their issues with authorities at similar times they can do so separately – even if in coordination – without having to choose one topic over the other. UN officials worry that the appointment of a single UN interlocutor to coordinate with the authorities on both immediate humanitarian priorities and longer-term political objectives could pit the new organisation’s teams against each other when deciding which issues should take higher priority in senior-level engagement. 153 The merger assessment considers this single interlocutor model to be a strength of the proposal, but UN officials consider it a weakness because of the potential trade-offs that would have to be made internally when deciding the priorities to be addressed in government engagement. Crisis Group interviews, UN officials, January-July 2026. Member states across the geographic and political spectrum have expressed concerns about the proposed merger. A coalition including Canada, Poland, South Korea and Sweden – which includes top contributors to both agencies – wrote to the Secretary-General saying they were “not in a position to support such a proposal” given the lack of clarity on how the two mandates could be safeguarded. 154 Canada letter to the UN Secretary-General , 15 May 2026. Separately, Russia and China also emphasised the need to protect the two mandates, albeit voicing different concerns. Russia pointed out that member states have no agreed-upon definition of “sexual rights”, saying it is therefore “inappropriate” for the proposed new entity to work in this domain. China, for its part, stressed that the process of merging two entities should be member state-led and transparent, suggesting that it objected to how the recommendation came about. 155 For more, see Letter from Russia to the UN Secretary-General , UNGA A/80/710, 20 April 2026; Remarks by China on the UN80 initiative , 8 June 2026. In response to requests from member state governing boards for alternative proposals, UN Women and UNFPA distributed their own papers, first in June and then in August, suggesting ways to align some of their work without a merger, including through shared data analytics and joint projects on gender-based violence in some locations. 156 The second of these papers also went into further detail on the costs of a merger, including the initial four-year financial impact ranging from a $9.9 million loss to a $38.2 million gain, after which savings could reach $35.1 million, depending on transition costs and organisational design. According to the UN’s own assessment of the merger, savings would be reinvested in the new entity. “ Further evidence and analysis on both the merger scenario and on alternative options to enhance alignment, impact and efficiency”, UN Women/UNFPA, 7 August 2026. Member states and UN officials should consider whether these proposals would satisfy the desire to increase efficiency without risking the mandate dilution implied by a merger. In so doing, they should shy away from politically ill-timed proposals that would threaten hard-won gains and could weaken UN support for women and girls in conflict and other crises in the long term. 9. Recasting discussions of the future of UN peace operations Diplomats routinely cite peace operations as one of the UN’s flagship contributions to peace and security. But the Security Council has not authorised a large-scale blue helmet force for over a decade, and the number of troops and police personnel serving under the organisation’s banner has halved in the same period. There have also been few new UN Special Political Missions (SPMs), which are solely or largely civilian in nature. As noted in the introduction, the Trump administration has pushed for budget cuts to UN missions of all kinds, questioning their expense, efficiency and apparent lack of concrete goals. To guide discussions about how to revitalise this atrophying tool, the Secretary-General published a review of all forms of peace operations. 157 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations: report of the Secretary General ”, UN General Assembly A/80/798 – UN Security Council S/2026/600, 22 July 2026. The review came out in August, having originally been requested by member states in late 2024. Though this study covers political missions – and makes a strong pitch for the UN to reinvest in prevention and good offices, discussed in the next section – many of its more technical recommendations are specific to operations with military and police components. A number of UN members, including the U.S., have complained that it says nothing startlingly new. 158 See, for example, “ The future of United Nations peace operations: Implementation of the recommendations of the High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations ”, UNGA A/70/357 – UNSC S/2015/682, 2 September 2015; “ Declaration of Shared Commitments on UN Peacekeeping Operations ”, UN Secretary-General, 16 August 2018; “ The Pact For The Future ”, UN General Assembly A/RES/79/1, 22 September 2024, paras 42(a)-42(g); “ Chair’s Summary – UN Peacekeeping Ministerial 2025 ”, 14 May 2025. But it is a solid overview of the challenges facing UN operations and a starting point for diplomatic discussions of solving them. UN missions face new challenges like disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks for which they are ill prepared. The report’s diagnosis of the problems facing peace operations is hard to dispute. As it notes, the UN is often tasked with propping up weak ceasefires and political processes amid endemic violence. UN missions face new challenges like disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks for which they are ill prepared. A divided and distracted Security Council provides limited political support for UN personnel on the ground and does not update their mandates in a timely fashion when they encounter changing threats (Council diplomats admit this judgment is fair). 159 “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10,137th Meeting of the UN Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10137, 15 April 2026. The Secretary-General stakes out a series of sensible, albeit technocratic, responses to these issues. He suggests that the Security Council should direct UN operations to find political approaches to ending and mitigating conflict; work out “compacts” with states defining shared commitments to making missions work; and take a flexible approach to reviewing and revising mandates. His paper calls for a further Secretariat report examining the capabilities UN missions need to become more agile, while hammering home the need for missions to become more cost-effective and accountable for their performance. UN staffers and diplomats will spend much of the year ahead following up on these proposals, but even if they can fix some of the process issues, broader political questions about the future of UN peace operations will remain. In today’s fraught geopolitical environment, the space for mediators – hailing from the UN or elsewhere – to craft sustainable peace processes will likely remain limited. 160 Crisis Group Briefing, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Security , op. cit. Embattled governments in regions such as the Sahel and countries like Haiti want international forces to neutralise their opponents rather than coax them to the negotiating table. Guterres and most UN officials agree that as a rule the UN should not become directly involved in peace enforcement, even if the Security Council backs ad hoc missions like the GSF in Haiti that the UN system can support logistically and administratively. The fundamental challenge facing the UN is to rebuild a case for conflict parties and other actors to invest in mediation processes and peacebuilding efforts that minimise violence, and that UN peace operations are qualified to offer these efforts support when useful. There may be an audience for this argument.
